Use `QueryMultiple` or `QueryMultipleAsync` when one command returns more than one result set. The callback receives an open query object that advances as each result is read.

```csharp
var sql = """
    select * from [User] where [EmailAddress] = @EmailAddress;
    select * from [Role];
    select * from [Priority];
    """;

User? user = null;
List<Role> roles = [];
List<Priority> priorities = [];

await session
    .Sql(sql)
    .Parameter("@EmailAddress", "kara.thrace@battlestar.com")
    .QueryMultipleAsync(async query =>
    {
        user = await query.QuerySingleAsync<User>(cancellationToken);
        roles = (await query.QueryAsync<Role>(cancellationToken)).ToList();
        priorities = (await query.QueryAsync<Priority>(cancellationToken)).ToList();
    }, cancellationToken);
```

Read the result sets in the same order the SQL command returns them.

## Query a DataTable

Use `QueryTable` or `QueryTableAsync` when a `DataTable` is the most convenient result format.

```csharp
var table = await session
    .Sql("select * from [User] where [IsDeleted] = @IsDeleted")
    .Parameter("@IsDeleted", false)
    .QueryTableAsync(cancellationToken);
```

## Read with IDataReader

Use `Read` or `ReadAsync` for complete control over the open `IDataReader`.

```csharp
var emails = new List<string>();

await session
    .Sql("select [EmailAddress] from [User] order by [EmailAddress]")
    .ReadAsync(async (reader, token) =>
    {
        while (await ((DbDataReader)reader).ReadAsync(token))
            emails.Add(reader.GetString("EmailAddress"));
    }, cancellationToken: cancellationToken);
```

The reader is disposed after the callback completes.

## Export JSON

Use `QueryJson` or `QueryJsonAsync` to execute a command and serialize the result set as a JSON array.

```csharp
var json = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .OrderBy(p => p.DisplayOrder)
        .Limit(0, 1000)
    )
    .QueryJsonAsync(cancellationToken: cancellationToken);
```

Write JSON directly to a stream for large exports.

```csharp
await using var stream = File.Create("status.json");

await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .OrderBy(p => p.DisplayOrder)
    )
    .QueryJsonAsync(stream, cancellationToken: cancellationToken);
```

Use `JsonWriterOptions` to control JSON writer behavior.

```csharp
var options = new JsonWriterOptions { Indented = true };

var json = session
    .Sql("select [Id], [Name] from [Status]")
    .QueryJson(options);
```

## Export CSV

Use `QueryCsv` or `QueryCsvAsync` to execute a command and serialize the result set as CSV.

```csharp
var csv = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .OrderBy(p => p.DisplayOrder)
        .Limit(0, 1000)
    )
    .QueryCsvAsync(cancellationToken);
```

Write CSV directly to a stream for large exports.

```csharp
await using var stream = File.Create("status.csv");

await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .OrderBy(p => p.DisplayOrder)
    )
    .QueryCsvAsync(stream, cancellationToken);
```

CSV output includes a header row and uses UTF-8 when writing to a stream.

## Command behavior

Factory-based query methods accept an optional `CommandBehavior` argument when you need to override the default reader behavior.

```csharp
var users = session
    .Sql("select * from [User]")
    .Query(
        reader => new User
        {
            Id = reader.GetGuid("Id"),
            EmailAddress = reader.GetString("EmailAddress")
        },
        CommandBehavior.SequentialAccess | CommandBehavior.SingleResult);
```

Generated entity queries use `SingleResult` and single-row generated queries also use `SingleRow`.

## Caching note

`Query`, `QuerySingle`, `QueryValue`, `QueryValues`, and `QueryTable` can use command caching when an `IDataCache` is configured and the command opts in with `UseCache`. `Execute`, `Read`, `QueryMultiple`, `QueryJson`, and `QueryCsv` are not cached.

---

# SQL Query Builder

Source: https://github.com/loresoft/fluentcommand/blob/master/docs/guide/sql.md

# SQL Query Builder

The SQL query builder creates parameterized `IDataCommand` instances from fluent builder expressions. It is useful when a query has optional filters, dynamic projections, provider-specific paging, insert/update output clauses, or an upsert shape that is easier to compose than hand-written SQL.

Use it from an `IDataSession` with `session.Sql(builder => ...)`, then execute the returned command with the normal query methods.

```csharp
await using var session = Services.GetRequiredService<IDataSession>();

var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Where(u => u.EmailAddress, "@battlestar.com", FilterOperators.Contains)
        .OrderBy(u => u.EmailAddress)
        .Limit(0, 10)
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

Builder values are added as command parameters such as `@p0000`. Table names, schemas, and column names are generated by the configured query generator. The SQL shown in this guide uses SQL Server-style quoting and paging; PostgreSQL and SQLite generators produce their own syntax where needed.

## Builder types

`Select<T>()`, `Insert<T>()`, `Update<T>()`, `Delete<T>()`, and `Upsert<T>()` use entity metadata such as `[Table]`, `[Column]`, `[Key]`, `[NotMapped]`, and database-generated properties. They also accept expression-based column selectors.

```csharp
var user = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Where(u => u.Id, userId)
    )
    .QuerySingleAsync<User>();
```

Use the non-generic builders when you want to supply table and column names directly.

```csharp
var count = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select()
        .Count()
        .From("User")
        .Where("IsDeleted", false)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<int>();
```

## Select rows

When no columns are selected, the builder emits `SELECT *`. Add `Column` or `Columns` calls for projections and aliases.

```csharp
var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Column(u => u.Id)
        .Column(u => u.DisplayName)
        .Column(u => u.EmailAddress)
        .Where(u => u.IsDeleted, false)
        .OrderBy(u => u.DisplayName)
        .Page(page: 1, pageSize: 25)
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
SELECT [Id], [DisplayName], [EmailAddress]
FROM [User]
WHERE ([IsDeleted] = @p0000)
ORDER BY [DisplayName] ASC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 25 ROWS ONLY;
```

Use `Limit(offset, size)` for explicit offsets, or `Page(page, pageSize)` for one-based page numbers. If the size or page size is less than or equal to zero, paging is not emitted.

## Filters

`Where` adds a parameterized predicate. The default operator is `FilterOperators.Equal`.

```csharp
var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Where(u => u.EmailAddress, "@battlestar.com", FilterOperators.Contains)
        .Where(u => u.AccessFailedCount, 3, FilterOperators.LessThanOrEqual)
        .Where(u => u.LockoutEnd, null, FilterOperators.IsNull)
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

Common operators are `Equal`, `NotEqual`, `LessThan`, `LessThanOrEqual`, `GreaterThan`, `GreaterThanOrEqual`, `StartsWith`, `EndsWith`, `Contains`, `IsNull`, `IsNotNull`, and `In`.

Use `WhereIn` for a list of values. Each item is emitted as its own parameter.

```csharp
var statusIds = new[] { 1, 2, 3 };

var statuses = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .WhereIn(s => s.Id, statusIds)
    )
    .QueryAsync<Status>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM [dbo].[Status]
WHERE ([Id] IN (@p0000,@p0001,@p0002));
```

Use `WhereIf` and `WhereInIf` for optional query criteria.

```csharp
var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .WhereIf(
            u => u.EmailAddress,
            emailFilter,
            FilterOperators.Contains,
            (_, value) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
        .WhereInIf(
            u => u.Id,
            selectedUserIds,
            (_, values) => values.Any())
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

Use `WhereOr` and `WhereAnd` to group predicates.

```csharp
var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Where(u => u.EmailAddress, "@battlestar.com", FilterOperators.Contains)
        .WhereOr(or => or
            .Where(u => u.IsDeleted, false)
            .Where(u => u.IsEmailAddressConfirmed, true)
        )
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM [User]
WHERE ([EmailAddress] LIKE '%' + @p0000 + '%' AND ([IsDeleted] = @p0001 OR [IsEmailAddressConfirmed] = @p0002));
```

## Joins

Join builders support table aliases and join types. For typed joins, the entity metadata supplies table and column names.

```csharp
var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Column(u => u.DisplayName, "u")
        .Column(u => u.EmailAddress, "u")
        .Column<Role>(r => r.Name, "r", "RoleName")
        .From(tableAlias: "u")
        .Join<UserRole>(join => join
            .Left(u => u.Id, "u")
            .Right(ur => ur.UserId, "ur")
        )
        .Join<UserRole, Role>(join => join
            .Left(ur => ur.RoleId, "ur")
            .Right(r => r.Id, "r")
        )
        .Where(u => u.EmailAddress, "@battlestar.com", "u", FilterOperators.Contains)
        .OrderBy(u => u.DisplayName, "u")
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
SELECT [u].[DisplayName], [u].[EmailAddress], [r].[Name] AS [RoleName]
FROM [User] AS [u]
INNER JOIN [UserRole] AS [ur] ON [u].[Id] = [ur].[UserId]
INNER JOIN [Role] AS [r] ON [ur].[RoleId] = [r].[Id]
WHERE ([u].[EmailAddress] LIKE '%' + @p0000 + '%')
ORDER BY [u].[DisplayName] ASC;
```

Set the join type with `.Type(JoinTypes.Left)`, `.Type(JoinTypes.Right)`, or another supported `JoinTypes` value.

## Aggregates and grouping

Use `Count` for row counts and `Aggregate` for aggregate functions such as `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, and `Max`.

```csharp
var activeCount = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .Count()
        .Where(s => s.IsActive, true)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<int>();
```

```csharp
var displayOrderTotal = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .Aggregate(s => s.DisplayOrder, AggregateFunctions.Sum, columnAlias: "TotalDisplayOrder")
        .GroupBy(s => s.IsActive)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<int>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
SELECT SUM([DisplayOrder]) AS [TotalDisplayOrder]
FROM [dbo].[Status]
GROUP BY [IsActive];
```

## Insert rows

Use `Value` to add explicit columns, or `Values(entity)` to include mapped, non-generated entity properties.

```csharp
var id = Guid.NewGuid();

var userId = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Insert<User>()
        .Value(u => u.Id, id)
        .Value(u => u.EmailAddress, $"{id}@email.com")
        .Value(u => u.DisplayName, "Last, First")
        .Output(u => u.Id)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<Guid>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
INSERT INTO [User] ([Id], [EmailAddress], [DisplayName])
OUTPUT [INSERTED].[Id]
VALUES (@p0000, @p0001, @p0002);
```

Insert an entity when the values already live in a model.

```csharp
var user = new User
{
    Id = Guid.NewGuid(),
    EmailAddress = "lee.adama@battlestar.com",
    DisplayName = "Adama, Lee",
    Created = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow,
    Updated = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow
};

await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Insert<User>()
        .Values(user)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

Pass column names to `Values(entity, columnNames)` when only part of an entity should be written.

## JSON values

`ValueJson` serializes a value to JSON before binding it as a command parameter. It is available on insert, update, and upsert builders.

```csharp
var audit = new
{
    Source = "Import",
    Count = 42,
    Created = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow
};

await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Insert()
        .Into("JsonLog")
        .Value("Id", Guid.NewGuid())
        .ValueJson("Data", audit)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
INSERT INTO [JsonLog] ([Id], [Data])
VALUES (@p0000, @p0001);
```

Use the overloads that accept `JsonSerializerOptions` or `JsonTypeInfo<T>` when you need custom serialization or source-generated JSON metadata.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Update()
        .Table("JsonLog")
        .ValueJson("Data", audit, AuditJsonContext.Default.AuditRecord)
        .Where("Id", logId)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

### Strongly typed JSON values

Typed entity builders (`Insert<TEntity>`, `Update<TEntity>`, and `Upsert<TEntity>`) support expression-based `ValueJson` overloads that select the target column from an entity property.

```csharp
[Table("Import", Schema = "dbo")]
public class ImportRecord
{
    [Key]
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public ImportMetadata Metadata { get; set; }
}

var metadata = new ImportMetadata
{
    Source = "Upload",
    Count = 100
};

var importId = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Insert<ImportRecord>()
        .Value(r => r.Id, 1)
        .ValueJson(r => r.Metadata, metadata)
        .Output(r => r.Id)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<int>();
```

The expression overload resolves the column name from entity metadata, so it stays consistent with the rest of the typed builder and is checked by the compiler.

Update and upsert work the same way.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Update<ImportRecord>()
        .ValueJson(r => r.Metadata, metadata)
        .Where(r => r.Id, importId)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Upsert<ImportRecord>()
        .Value(r => r.Id, 1)
        .ValueJson(r => r.Metadata, metadata)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

Use `JsonSerializerOptions` or `JsonTypeInfo<T>` with the expression overloads when you need custom serialization.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Insert<ImportRecord>()
        .Value(r => r.Id, 1)
        .ValueJson(r => r.Metadata, metadata, ImportJsonContext.Default.ImportMetadata)
        .Output(r => r.Id)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<int>();
```

## Update rows

Update builders combine `Value`, optional `Output`, and `Where` clauses. Always include a filter unless you intentionally want to update every row.

```csharp
var updatedId = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Update<User>()
        .Value(u => u.DisplayName, "Updated")
        .ValueIf(u => u.LastLogin, lastLogin, (_, value) => value.HasValue)
        .Output(u => u.Id)
        .Where(u => u.Id, userId)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<Guid>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
UPDATE [User]
SET [DisplayName] = @p0000, [LastLogin] = @p0001
OUTPUT [INSERTED].[Id]
WHERE ([Id] = @p0002);
```

For update statements that depend on another table, use `From` and `Join` with aliases.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Update<User>()
        .Table("User", tableAlias: "u")
        .Value(u => u.IsEmailAddressConfirmed, true)
        .From(tableAlias: "u")
        .Join<UserRole>(join => join
            .Left(u => u.Id, "u")
            .Right(ur => ur.UserId, "ur")
        )
        .Where<UserRole, Guid>(ur => ur.RoleId, roleId, "ur")
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

## Delete rows

Delete builders support typed filters, joins, and output columns. Always include a `Where` clause unless you intentionally want to delete every row.

```csharp
var deletedId = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Delete<User>()
        .Output(u => u.Id)
        .Where(u => u.Id, userId)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<Guid>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
DELETE FROM [User]
OUTPUT [DELETED].[Id]
WHERE ([Id] = @p0000);
```

Use the non-generic builder when the table name is not represented by a mapped entity.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Delete()
        .Table("JsonLog")
        .Where("Created", cutoff, FilterOperators.LessThan)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

## Upsert rows

Upsert builders insert a row when the key does not exist and update non-key values when it does. SQL Server output uses `MERGE`; other providers generate equivalent provider-specific SQL.

With explicit table and column names, define at least one key and at least one non-key value.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Upsert()
        .Into("Status", "dbo")
        .Key("Id")
        .Value("Id", 1)
        .Value("Name", "Upsert Status")
        .Value("Description", "Inserted or updated")
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
MERGE INTO [dbo].[Status] AS TARGET
USING (VALUES (@p0000, @p0001, @p0002)) AS SOURCE
([Id], [Name], [Description])
ON TARGET.[Id] = SOURCE.[Id]
WHEN MATCHED THEN
UPDATE SET TARGET.[Name] = SOURCE.[Name], TARGET.[Description] = SOURCE.[Description]
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
INSERT ([Id], [Name], [Description])
VALUES (SOURCE.[Id], SOURCE.[Name], SOURCE.[Description]);
```

Typed upserts infer keys from `[Key]` properties when you call `Values(entity)`.

```csharp
[Table("Status", Schema = "dbo")]
public class StatusUpsert
{
    [Key]
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; } = null!;

    public string? Description { get; set; }
}

var status = new StatusUpsert
{
    Id = 1,
    Name = "Upsert Entity",
    Description = "Inserted or updated"
};

var statusId = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Upsert<StatusUpsert>()
        .Values(status)
        .Output(s => s.Id)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<int>();
```

Use `Key`, `KeyIf`, `Value`, `ValueIf`, and `ValueJson` when you need more control than `Values(entity)`.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Upsert()
        .Into("JsonLog")
        .Key("Id")
        .Value("Id", logId)
        .ValueJson("Data", audit)
        .Output("Id")
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<Guid>();
```

## Output clauses

`Output` is available on insert, update, delete, and upsert builders. It lets you return generated or affected values and read them with `QueryValue`, `QuerySingle`, or `Query`.

```csharp
var id = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Insert<User>()
        .Values(user)
        .Output(u => u.Id)
    )
    .QueryValueAsync<Guid>();
```

Use `OutputIf` when output should be included only for specific flows.

```csharp
var command = session.Sql(builder => builder
    .Update<User>()
    .Value(u => u.DisplayName, displayName)
    .OutputIf(u => u.Id, condition: _ => returnUpdatedId)
    .Where(u => u.Id, userId));
```

## Raw statements and mixed batches

Use `Statement()` to include raw SQL in the same builder batch. Parameters added to a statement are shared with the generated statements in the batch.

```csharp
var values = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.ToDelimitedString();

var statuses = await session
    .Sql(builder =>
    {
        builder
            .Statement()
            .Query("CREATE TABLE #identifiers (Id int);");

        builder
            .Statement()
            .Query("INSERT INTO #identifiers (Id) SELECT CONVERT(int, value) FROM STRING_SPLIT(@Identifiers, @Separator);")
            .Parameter("@Identifiers", values)
            .Parameter("@Separator", ",");

        builder
            .Select<Status>()
            .From(tableAlias: "s")
            .Join(join => join
                .Left("Id", "s")
                .Right("Id", "#identifiers", null, "i"));
    })
    .QueryAsync<Status>();
```

Generated output:

```sql
CREATE TABLE #identifiers (Id int);
INSERT INTO #identifiers (Id) SELECT CONVERT(int, value) FROM STRING_SPLIT(@Identifiers, @Separator);
SELECT *
FROM [dbo].[Status] AS [s]
INNER JOIN [#identifiers] AS [i] ON [s].[Id] = [i].[Id];
```

Raw helpers are also available for selected clauses, including `FromRaw`, `WhereRaw`, and `OrderByRaw`. Prefer the typed and parameterized methods for user input, and reserve raw clauses for trusted SQL fragments.

## Tags and comments

`Tag()` adds a provider-formatted SQL comment with the caller name, source file, and line number. This is useful when query logging is enabled.

```csharp
var statuses = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<Status>()
        .Where(s => s.IsActive, true)
        .Tag()
    )
    .QueryAsync<Status>();
```

Example SQL:

```sql
/* Caller; GetStatusesAsync() in StatusRepository.cs:line 42 */
SELECT *
FROM [dbo].[Status]
WHERE ([IsActive] = @p0000);
```

Use `Tag("Custom label")` for a custom caller label, or `Comment("text")` when you want only a literal SQL comment.

## Execution

The builder only creates the command text and parameters. The returned `IDataCommand` can be executed with the same APIs as hand-written SQL.

```csharp
await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Update<User>()
        .Value(u => u.LastLogin, DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)
        .Where(u => u.Id, userId)
    )
    .ExecuteAsync();
```

```csharp
var users = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Where(u => u.IsDeleted, false)
    )
    .QueryAsync<User>();
```

```csharp
var json = await session
    .Sql(builder => builder
        .Select<User>()
        .Where(u => u.IsDeleted, false)
    )
    .QueryJsonAsync();
```

You can still add normal command options after the builder call, such as `CommandTimeout`, additional parameters for raw statements, or other `IDataCommand` configuration.

# FluentCommand

Source: https://github.com/loresoft/fluentcommand/blob/master/docs/index.md

# FluentCommand

Fluent wrapper for ADO.NET `DbCommand` with automatic object mapping, caching, query building, and source-generated data readers.



| Package | Version |
| :--- | :--- |
| [FluentCommand](https://www.nuget.org/packages/FluentCommand/) | [![FluentCommand](https://img.shields.io/nuget/v/FluentCommand.svg)](https://www.nuget.org/packages/FluentCommand/) |
| [FluentCommand.SqlServer](https://www.nuget.org/packages/FluentCommand.SqlServer/) | [![FluentCommand.SqlServer](https://img.shields.io/nuget/v/FluentCommand.SqlServer.svg)](https://www.nuget.org/packages/FluentCommand.SqlServer/) |
| [FluentCommand.Caching](https://www.nuget.org/packages/FluentCommand.Caching/) | [![FluentCommand.Caching](https://img.shields.io/nuget/v/FluentCommand.Caching.svg)](https://www.nuget.org/packages/FluentCommand.Caching/) |

## Installation

```shell
dotnet add package FluentCommand
```

For SQL Server bulk copy, merge, and import features:

```shell
dotnet add package FluentCommand.SqlServer
```

For distributed caching:

```shell
dotnet add package FluentCommand.Caching
```

## Features

- Fluent wrapper over `DbConnection` and `DbCommand`
- Automatic connection state management
- Source-generated `IDataReader` mapping (no reflection)
- SQL query builder with Select, Insert, Update, Delete, and Upsert support
- JSON column support with `[JsonColumn]` attribute for source-generated readers
- JSON and CSV export directly from query results
- JSON parameter serialization with `ParameterJson`
- Parameterized queries with output, input-output, and return value callbacks
- Conditional parameters and query builder filters (`ParameterIf`, `WhereIf`, `ValueIf`)
- Result caching with sliding or absolute expiration
- Distributed cache integration via `FluentCommand.Caching`
- Query logging with elapsed time and parameter details
- Connection and command interceptors
- Multiple result set handling
- Multiple database configuration with discriminated registrations
- SQL Server bulk copy and merge data operations
- Tabular data import with field mapping, validation, and merge
- Multi-target: `netstandard2.0`, `net8.0`, `net9.0`, `net10.0`
- Supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and SQLite
